text: The applicants are a group of individuals and the Foundation for Equality.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The first applicant is a member of the executive committee of the Foundation for Equality and is empowered to act on its behalf in the present case.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The applicants wished to hold an assembly (a march) in Warsaw within the framework of Equality Days organised by the Foundation for Equality, planned for 10-12 June 2005.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The purpose of the planned march in Warsaw was to alert public opinion to the issue of discrimination against minorities – sexual, national, ethnic and religious – and also against women and disabled persons.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: On 10 May 2005 the organisers held a meeting with the Director of the Safety and Crisis Management Unit of Warsaw City Council.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: During the meeting on 10 May 2005 between the organisers and the Director of the Safety and Crisis Management Unit of Warsaw City Council, an initial agreement was reached as to the itinerary of the planned march.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: On 11 May 2005 Mr Bączkowski obtained an instruction of the Warsaw Mayor's Office on requirements which organisers of public assemblies have to comply with under the Road Traffic Act, applicable should the assembly be regarded as an 'event' (impreza) within the meaning of Article 65 of the Road Traffic Act.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: On 12 May 2005 the organisers applied to the City Council Road Traffic Office for permission to organise the march.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The itinerary of the planned march would lead from the Parliament buildings (Sejm) to Assembly Square (Plac Defilad) in the centre of Warsaw.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: On 3 June 2005 the Traffic Officer, acting on behalf of the Mayor of Warsaw, refused permission for the march.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The Traffic Officer's refusal of permission for the march on 3 June 2005 was based on the organisers' failure to submit a 'traffic organisation plan' ('projekt organizacji ruchu') within the meaning of Article 65(a) of the Road Traffic Act.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The Traffic Officer alleged that the organisers had been ordered to submit a 'traffic organisation plan' ('projekt organizacji ruchu') prior to the refusal of 3 June 2005.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: On 3 June 2005 the applicants informed the Mayor of Warsaw about stationary assemblies they intended to hold on 11 June 2005 in seven different squares in Warsaw.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: Four of the seven planned stationary assemblies on 11 June 2005 were intended to protest about discrimination against various minorities and to support actions of groups and organisations combating discrimination.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: Three of the seven planned stationary assemblies on 11 June 2005 were intended to protest about discrimination against women.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: On 9 June 2005 the Mayor of Warsaw issued decisions banning the stationary assemblies to be organised by Mr Bączkowski, Mr Biedroń, Mr Kliszczyński, Ms Kostrzewa, Mr Szypuła, and Mr N. (who is not an applicant).
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: Mr Bączkowski, Mr Biedroń, Mr Kliszczyński, Ms Kostrzewa, Mr Szypuła, and Mr N. are active in various non-governmental organisations acting for the benefit of persons of homosexual orientation.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: In his decision of 9 June 2005 banning the stationary assemblies, the Mayor of Warsaw relied on the argument that assemblies held under the provisions of the 1990 Assemblies Act (Ustawa o zgromadzeniach) had to be organised away from roads used for road traffic.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: In his decision of 9 June 2005, the Mayor of Warsaw stated that if assemblies were to use roads, more stringent requirements applied.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The organisers of the stationary assemblies wished to use cars carrying loudspeakers.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The organisers had failed to indicate where and how the cars carrying loudspeakers would park during the assemblies so as not to disturb traffic.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The organisers had failed to indicate how the movement of persons and cars between the assembly sites would be organised.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: A number of requests had been submitted to organise other assemblies on 11 June 2005, the tenor of which ran counter to the ideas and intentions of the applicants.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The Mayor of Warsaw refused permission for the applicants' stationary assemblies in part to avoid possible violent clashes between participants in the various demonstrations planned for 11 June 2005.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: On 9 June 2005 the municipal authorities, acting on the Mayor of Warsaw's behalf, allowed the three planned stationary assemblies concerning discrimination against women to be held as requested by the applicants.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: On 9 June 2005 the municipal authorities, acting on the Mayor of Warsaw's behalf, permitted six other demonstrations to be held on 11 June 2005.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The six other demonstrations permitted on 9 June 2005 to be held on 11 June 2005 had the following themes: 'For more stringent measures against persons convicted of paedophilia', 'Against any legislative work on the law on partnerships', 'Against propaganda for partnerships', 'Education in Christian values, a guarantee of a moral society', 'Christians respecting God's and nature's laws are citizens of the first rank', and 'Against adoption of children by homosexual couples'.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: On 11 June 2005, despite the decision of 3 June 2005 refusing permission, the march took place.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The march on 11 June 2005 followed the itinerary as planned in the original request of 12 May 2005.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The march on 11 June 2005 was attended by approximately 3,000 people.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The march on 11 June 2005 was protected by the police.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: On 11 June 2005, nine stationary assemblies were held in addition to the march, under permission granted by the Mayor of Warsaw on 9 June 2005.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: On 28 June 2005 the applicant Foundation for Equality appealed to the Local Government Appeals Board against the decision of 3 June 2005 refusing permission for the march.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: In its appeal of 28 June 2005, the applicant Foundation for Equality argued that the requirement to submit a 'traffic organisation plan' lacked any legal basis.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: In its appeal of 28 June 2005, the applicant Foundation for Equality argued that the applicants had never been requested to submit a 'traffic organisation plan' prior to the refusal of 3 June 2005.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: In its appeal of 28 June 2005, the applicant Foundation for Equality argued that the decision of 3 June 2005 amounted to an unwarranted restriction of freedom of assembly.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: In its appeal of 28 June 2005, the applicant Foundation for Equality argued that the decision of 3 June 2005 had been dictated by ideological reasons incompatible with the tenets of democracy.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: On 22 August 2005 the Local Government Appeals Board quashed the decision of 3 June 2005 refusing permission for the march, finding that it was unlawful.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The Local Government Appeals Board observed that under the applicable provisions of administrative procedure the authorities were obliged to ensure that parties to administrative proceedings had an opportunity of effectively participating in them.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The Local Government Appeals Board found that the obligation to ensure effective participation in administrative proceedings had not been respected in the applicant Foundation for Equality's case, in that the case file contained no evidence that the applicant Foundation for Equality had been informed of its procedural right to have access to the case file.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The Local Government Appeals Board found that the first-instance authority's decision of 3 June 2005 referred to the absence of a traffic organisation plan in the case file, but that the case file contained no mention that the organisers had been obliged to submit such a plan.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The Local Government Appeals Board found that the document on the procedure for obtaining permission to organise an event which was served on the organisers contained no information on the obligation to submit a traffic organisation plan.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The Local Government Appeals Board noted that the organisers' request concerned a march to be held on 11 June 2005 and that the appeal was received by the Board's Office together with the case file on 28 June 2005, by which date the proceedings had already become devoid of purpose.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: On 10 June 2005 the applicants appealed to the Mazowsze Governor against the Mayor of Warsaw's refusals of 9 June 2005 of permission to hold several of the planned stationary assemblies.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: In their appeal of 10 June 2005, the applicants argued that the assemblies were to be entirely peaceful and that banning them breached their freedom of assembly guaranteed by the Constitution.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: In their appeal of 10 June 2005, the applicants submitted that the assemblies did not pose any threat to either public order or morals.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: In their appeal of 10 June 2005, the applicants contested the argument relied on in the Mayor of Warsaw's decision that they were required to submit a document on the planned itinerary between the places where the assemblies were to be held.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: In their appeal of 10 June 2005, the applicants argued that they only intended to organise stationary assemblies, not any movement of persons between them, and that they should not be held responsible for the organisation or supervision of such movement.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: On 17 June 2005 the Mazowsze Governor quashed the Mayor of Warsaw's refusals of 9 June 2005 of authorisation to hold the stationary assemblies.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The Mazowsze Governor observed that the Mayor of Warsaw's decisions of 9 June 2005 breached the law in that the parties had been served only with copies of the decisions, not with originals as required by the law on administrative procedure.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The Mazowsze Governor noted that the Mayor of Warsaw had informed the media of his decisions of 9 June 2005 before they had been served on the applicants, which was manifestly in breach of the principles of administrative procedure.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The Mazowsze Governor observed that the 1990 Assemblies Act was a guarantee of freedom of assembly in respect of both the organisation of and participation in assemblies.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The Mazowsze Governor observed that the Constitution clearly guaranteed freedom of assembly, not a right, and that it was not for the State to create a right to assembly; its obligation was limited to ensuring that assemblies were held peacefully.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The Mazowsze Governor observed that the applicable law did not provide for any permit for the holding of an assembly.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The Mazowsze Governor noted that the requirement to submit a permit to occupy a part of the road, based on the provisions of the Road Traffic Act, lacked any legal basis in the provisions of the 1990 Assemblies Act.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The Mazowsze Governor noted that the Mayor of Warsaw had assumed that the demonstration would occupy a part of the road, but had failed to take any steps to clarify whether this had really been the organisers' intention, which he was obliged to do by law.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The Mazowsze Governor observed that a decision banning an assembly had to be regarded as a method of last resort because it radically restricted freedom of expression.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The Mazowsze Governor observed that the principle of proportionality required that any restriction of constitutionally protected freedoms be permitted only in so far as it was dictated by the concrete circumstances of a particular case.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The Mazowsze Governor noted that the Mayor of Warsaw's reliance on the threat of violence between the demonstrations organised by the applicants and the counter-demonstrations planned by other persons and organisations for 11 June 2005 could not be countenanced.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The Mazowsze Governor stated that the Mayor of Warsaw's reliance on the threat of violence was tantamount to the administration endorsing the intentions of organisations which clearly and deliberately intended to breach public order.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The Mazowsze Governor stated that protecting the freedom of expression guaranteed by the 1990 Assemblies Act should be an essential task of the public powers.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: The Mazowsze Governor discontinued the proceedings concerning the stationary assemblies as they had become devoid of purpose, the assemblies having taken place on 11 June 2005.
section_path: I. THE CIRCUMSTANCES OF THE CASE

text: Article 57 of the Polish Constitution provides that freedom of peaceful assembly and participation in such assemblies shall be ensured to everyone, and that limitations upon such freedoms may be imposed by statute.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Article 79 § 1 of the Polish Constitution entered into force on 17 October 1997.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Article 79 § 1 of the Polish Constitution provides that everyone whose constitutional freedoms or rights have been infringed shall have the right to appeal to the Constitutional Court for a judgment on the conformity with the Constitution of a statute or other normative act on the basis of which a court or an administrative authority has issued a final decision on his freedoms or rights or on his obligations specified in the Constitution, in accordance with principles specified by statute.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Article 190 § 1 of the Polish Constitution provides that judgments of the Constitutional Court shall be universally binding and final.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Article 190 § 2 of the Polish Constitution provides that judgments of the Constitutional Court shall be published without delay.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Article 190 § 3 of the Polish Constitution provides that a judgment of the Constitutional Court shall take effect from the day of its publication, but that the Constitutional Court may specify another date for the end of the binding force of a normative act, with such time-limit not exceeding 18 months in relation to a statute or 12 months in relation to any other normative act.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Pursuant to section 1 of the 1990 Assemblies Act, everyone has the right to freedom of peaceful assembly.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Under section 1 of the 1990 Assemblies Act, a gathering of at least fifteen persons, called in order to participate in a public debate or to express an opinion on a given issue, is to be regarded as an assembly within the meaning of the Act.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Under section 2 of the 1990 Assemblies Act, freedom of assembly can be restricted only by statute and where it is necessary for the protection of national security or public safety, for the protection of health or morals, or for the protection of the rights and freedoms of others.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Under the 1990 Assemblies Act, all decisions concerning the exercise of freedom of assembly must be taken by the local authorities in the municipality where the assembly is to be held.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Under the 1990 Assemblies Act, decisions concerning the exercise of freedom of assembly can be appealed against to the Governor.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Under section 3 of the 1990 Assemblies Act, the municipality must be informed by the organisers of the intention to hold a public gathering in the open air for an indeterminate number of persons.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Under section 7 of the 1990 Assemblies Act, information about a planned public gathering must be submitted to the municipality not earlier than thirty days before the planned date of the demonstration and not later than three days before it.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Under section 7 of the 1990 Assemblies Act, the information submitted to the municipality must include the names and addresses of the organisers, the aim and programme of the demonstration, its place, date and time, and information about the itinerary if the demonstration is intended to proceed from one place to another.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Pursuant to section 8 of the 1990 Assemblies Act, the municipality shall refuse permission for a demonstration if its purpose is in breach of the 1990 Assemblies Act itself or of provisions of the Criminal Code, or if the demonstration might entail a danger to life or limb, or a major danger to property.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Under the 1990 Assemblies Act, a first-instance refusal of permission to hold a demonstration must be served on the organisers within three days of the date on which the relevant request was submitted and not later than three days before the planned date of the demonstration.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Under the 1990 Assemblies Act, an appeal against a first-instance refusal of permission to hold a demonstration must be lodged within three days of the date of its service.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Under the 1990 Assemblies Act, the lodging of an appeal against a refusal of permission to hold a demonstration does not have a suspensive effect on the refusal.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Under the 1990 Assemblies Act, a decision given by the appellate authority must be served on the organisers within three days of the date on which the appeal was submitted.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Under section 65 of the Road Traffic Act of 1997, as amended in 2003, the organisers of sporting events, contests, assemblies and other events which may obstruct road traffic are obliged to obtain permission for the organisation of such assemblies.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Under section 65 read together with section 65(a) of the Road Traffic Act of 1997, as amended in 2003, organisers of events which may obstruct road traffic are obliged to comply with various administrative obligations specified in a list contained in section 65(a), numbering nineteen items, including the obligation to submit a traffic organisation plan to the authorities.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: The provisions of sections 65 and 65(a) of the Road Traffic Act of 1997, as amended in 2003, were repealed as a result of the judgment of the Constitutional Court of 18 January 2006.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: In its judgment of 18 January 2006, the Constitutional Court examined a request submitted by the Ombudsman to determine whether the requirements imposed on organisers of public events by the provisions of the Road Traffic Act were compatible with the Constitution in so far as they impinged on freedom of assembly, or whether they amounted to an excessive limitation of that freedom.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
4. Judgment of the Constitutional Court of 18 January 2006

text: The Constitutional Court observed that the essence of the constitutional problem was whether the requirements imposed by section 65 of the Road Traffic Act were compatible with freedom of expression as formulated by the Constitution and developed by the 1990 Assemblies Act.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
4. Judgment of the Constitutional Court of 18 January 2006

text: The Constitutional Court noted that the 1990 Assemblies Act was based on the premise that the exercise of freedom of assembly did not require any authorisations or licences issued by the State.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
4. Judgment of the Constitutional Court of 18 January 2006

text: The Constitutional Court noted that freedom of assembly being a freedom meant the State was obliged to refrain from hindering its exercise and to ensure that it was enjoyed by various groups despite the fact that their views might not be shared by the majority.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
4. Judgment of the Constitutional Court of 18 January 2006

text: The Constitutional Court observed that the 1990 Assemblies Act provided for a system based on nothing more than the registration of the proposed assembly.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
4. Judgment of the Constitutional Court of 18 January 2006

text: The Constitutional Court observed that when the legislature enacted the Road Traffic Act, it incorporated various administrative requirements which were difficult to comply with into the procedure created for the organisation of sporting events, contests and assemblies, thus replacing the registration system by a system based on permission.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
4. Judgment of the Constitutional Court of 18 January 2006

text: The Constitutional Court observed that the Road Traffic Act placed assemblies within the meaning of the 1990 Assemblies Act on a par with events of a commercial character or organised for entertainment purposes.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
4. Judgment of the Constitutional Court of 18 January 2006

text: The Constitutional Court found that placing assemblies on a par with commercial or entertainment events was incompatible with the special position that freedom of expression occupied in a democratic society and rendered nugatory the special place that assemblies had in the legal system under the Constitution and the 1990 Assemblies Act.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
4. Judgment of the Constitutional Court of 18 January 2006

text: The Constitutional Court noted that the list of requirements imposed by the Road Traffic Act contained as many as nineteen sundry administrative obligations.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
4. Judgment of the Constitutional Court of 18 January 2006

text: The Constitutional Court found that the restrictions on freedom of assembly imposed by the Road Traffic Act were in breach of the requirement of proportionality applicable to all restrictions imposed on the rights guaranteed by the Constitution.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
4. Judgment of the Constitutional Court of 18 January 2006

text: The Constitutional Court concluded in its judgment of 18 January 2006 that section 65 of the Road Traffic Act was incompatible with the Constitution in so far as it applied to assemblies.
section_path: II. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
4. Judgment of the Constitutional Court of 18 January 2006
